title: TF module versioning + registry publish + upgrade cheat-sheet
body:
Goal: give a tight, practical checklist and migration plan for publishing Terraform modules used in Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments, with a clear approach for versioning, registry publishes, and handling breaking changes across customer upgrade waves.

Context and principles:
- Private deployments rely on pinned module versions in customer stacks; upgrades are customer-facing and must be predictable.
- Keep backward compatibility as first-class: prefer non-breaking minor releases. When breaking changes are unavoidable, provide a migration path and a staged rollout plan.
- Automate detection where possible: CI should run compatibility tests and a lightweight schema diff.

What counts as a breaking change (heuristics):
- Removal or renaming of public inputs/outputs (input/variable name changes, output name removal).
- Changing default values that alter behavior in ways that could change resource topology (e.g., default instance types, subnetwork cidr changes).
- Resource address changes (moving resources between modules that change resource addresses in state).
- Changing type constraints in a way that would reject previously-valid values (string -> object, for instance).
- Changing lifecycle semantics (adding create_before_destroy without migration testing).

Semantic versioning rules (practical):
- MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH but with strong behavioral guidance:
  - PATCH: bugfixes, docs, test-only changes, non-functional refactors. Safe to release without customer coordination.
  - MINOR: backwards-compatible new features (new optional variables, additional outputs), performance improvements. Can be released with normal registry publish; recommend announcing in release notes and changelog.
  - MAJOR: any breaking change per the heuristics. Requires migration guide + coordinated rollout.

Pre-publish checklist (CI + human):
- Run unit + acceptance tests across supported Terraform versions (at least TF 1.3, 1.5, latest). (CI step: tf test matrix)
- Run automated compatibility diff tool (script: tools/tf-compat-checker) comparing current module interface to previous tag.
- Ensure all variables have descriptions and sensible defaults. Add deprecation notes to variables being phased out.
- Validate examples/consumers in examples/ directory against the new module tag.
- Changelog: fill in CHANGELOG.md with bullet summary of user-facing changes.
- Release notes draft: indicate migration steps for breaking changes under MAJOR.
- Tag and sign release: git tag vX.Y.Z and push; attach any generated docs to the registry entry.

Registry publish steps (Terraform Registry or self-hosted registry):
- For public registry: ensure module name, owners, and version constraints are set.
- For private/internal registry (we often use a private registry proxy):
  1) Create a release in GitHub with the tag and changelog.
  2) CI will generate an archive and push metadata to the registry API endpoint.
  3) Upload supplementary artifacts: example stacks, migration guide, and automated test outputs.
- Post-publish smoke check: CI runs examples against the published registry version and a minimal consumer stack.

Breaking-change playbook (when MAJOR required):
- Preconditions: technical justification (short explainer), migration plan, updated examples, test coverage, and runbook for support.
- Stakeholder notif: Send a short announcement to #private-deployments (Slack), customer-success, and account owners for any customers using the module (list obtainable from customer module usage dashboard).
- Draft migration guide with concrete before/after snippets. Add at the top: TL;DR, impact summary, estimated time for customer migration, and rollback steps.
- Release gating: do not publish MAJOR to the public registry until internal canary upgrades succeed.
- Canary wave plan:
  Wave 0 (internal): upgrade internal testbeds, CI, and our own private deployment overlays.
  Wave 1 (opt-in customers): 1–3 low-risk customers who agreed to early upgrades. Perform upgrade with engineering watching logs.
  Wave 2 (non-critical customers): customers with staging environments; schedule upgrades during maintenance windows.
  Wave 3 (general availability): broader publish and recommend the new tag.
- Rollback: keep the previous MAJOR available and maintain compatibility docs for toggling back. If stateformat changes occurred, provide exact terraform state mv steps and example sequences.

Upgrade runbook (operator checklist for upgrading a private deployment):
- Backup: ensure a snapshot of the control plane and Terraform state is taken (s3/gs/az blob + locking).
- Read the migration guide and note any manual steps.
- Dry run: terraform plan against a replica environment.
- Apply to staging; validate service-level smoke tests (API health, DB migrations, etc.).
- Monitor for 24–48h for regressions before rolling to production.
- If failure, run documented rollback steps: terraform apply with previous tag, any state moves, and verification steps.

Testing matrix suggestions (CI):
- Matrix axes: terraform version, provider versions (aws, azurerm, k8s), module feature flags (eg disable optional resources).
- Add acceptance tests that instantiate module examples with minimal and full config to detect default-changes.
- Add a delta test: run consumer stacks against both old and new module versions and compare plan diffs (zero unintended changes expected for non-breaking releases).

Example changelog template (what we publish):
- vX.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)
  - Highlights: 2–3 bullets with user impact.
  - Migration notes: short actionable snippet if MAJOR.
  - Example: before -> after (code block).
  - CI verification checklist: list of tests run.

Automation ideas (low-effort, high-value):
- Add a CI job that produces a semantic diff of variables/outputs between tags and fails if it detects a potential breaking change unless a MAJOR bump is present.
- Auto-generate a migration skeleton in docs/ when PR includes variable deletions/renames.
- Customer-usage exporter: script to map which customers use which module version so CS/product can coordinate upgrades.

Support/communication templates (short):
- Slack alert (to #private-deployments): "[ModuleX] vA.B.C -> vX.Y.Z released. Breaking: yes/no. Action: see migration guide <link>. Canary wave started: wave 0/1"
- Customer email: one-paragraph impact, scheduled maintenance window options, opt-in link, and rollback assurance.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we require automated compatibility diff to be a gating job on PRs for modules (currently recommended but optional)?
- Do we need a formal deprecation window policy (e.g., 90 days notice) for inputs/outputs? (Proposal: 90–180 days depending on impact)
- Who owns the customer-usage exporter and where does it run? (Ops or Solutions Eng?)

Notes to self / quick commands:
- Build + test locally: make test MODULE=private/vpc MODULE_EXAMPLE=basic
- Create release: git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin --tags && gh release create vX.Y.Z --notes-file CHANGELOG.md
- Run compat check: python tools/tf_compat_check.py --from-tag vOld --to-tag vNew --format brief

Appendix: short migration snippet examples
- Renaming a variable without breaking (recommended pattern):
  1) Introduce new variable 'new_name' with same default and mark old variable 'old_name' as deprecated in description.
  2) In module internals, prefer new_name if set else fallback to old_name.
  3) Release MINOR that documents upcoming removal.
  4) After deprecation window, remove old_name in MAJOR.

- Example terraform state move command for resource address changes:
  terraform state mv 'module.old_module.aws_db_instance.main' 'module.new_module.aws_db_instance.main'
  (include lock+backup steps and test in staging)

End: Please review for gaps especially around legal/regulatory constraints for private (on-prem) customers — several customers require longer deprecation windows; we should collate those account exceptions and add to the customer-usage exporter.

Signed: Priya
